He didn't get into acting until late in high school, and his acting teacher made him do genres other than comedy to get experience with what he wasn't already comfortable with.

entertainment.title: 10 Best Medieval Fantasy Shows Of All Time, Ranked
entertainment.summary: The fantasy genre and medieval settings tend to go hand in hand. Let's break down the 10 greatest medieval fantasy shows of all time.
entertainment.body:
HBO Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Maybe it's the "Dungeons & Dragons" fan in all of us, but there is an undeniable appeal to fantasy stories evoking the European medieval area. That iconic juxtaposition of sword-wielding knights and sorcerers in expansive realms saliently evokes the classic archetypes of the genre. Whether its retellings of Arthurian legend or shows riffing on the work of author J.R.R. Tolkien, there is no shortage of medieval fantasy shows. We're taking a look at our personal favorite medieval fantasy series, both in live-action and animation as the genre continues to thrive.

Many of the best fantasy television shows ever made happen to be those in a visibly medieval setting. The iconography that comes from these aesthetics are often too rich to pass up and really elevate these types of stories. Many of the shows that we're listing here also happen to be literary adaptations, with best-selling authors using these elements well to widespread fan appreciation. These are the 10 best medieval fantasy shows of all time, exemplifying the appeal of the popular sub-genre.

Trigger/Netflix Let's start off this list with a memorable recent anime series that takes a gastronomic approach to the medieval fantasy genre. Ryoko Kui's manga series "Delicious in Dungeon" was adapted for television in 2024 and is currently available to stream on Netflix. The story follows adventurer Laios Touden who leads an expedition into a sprawling dungeon to rescue his sister from a dragon. Laios also takes the opportunity to try out cooking recipes from fantasy creatures he encounters and slays like mandrakes and animated suits of armor.

If you've ever wondered how to cook certain types of classic fantasy monsters, "Delicious in Dungeon" answers those culinary questions. This odd juxtaposition between medieval action and cooking sequences fuels a lot of the show's self-aware sense of humor. But once the series establishes its strange premise, it brings its more conventionally character-driven fantasy narrative to the forefront. While it may seem silly at first glance, "Delicious in Dungeon" celebrates the genre while providing cooking scenes that are just as entertaining as the combat.

Netflix While "The Witcher" has been a decidedly uneven production, largely due to the departure of Henry Cavill as the show's protagonist, the show still delivers top-notch fantasy action. An adaptation of Andrzej Sapkowski's novel series, the story centers on Geralt of Rivia, a monster hunter known as a Witcher. Geralt's life is changed when he adopts Ciri (Freya Allen), who is targeted for the magical potential in her blood. Cavill plays Geralt for the first three seasons while Liam Hemsworth plays the character for the show's final two seasons.

entertainment.title: Tom Selleck Landed Magnum P.I. Thanks To A Western Miniseries With Sam Elliot
entertainment.summary: Magnum, P.I. turned Tom Selleck into a household name, but he never would have gone down in history as a TV legend if he hadn't crossed paths with Sam Elliot.
entertainment.body:
CBS Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Back in the '80s, Tom Selleck rose to fame for his role as Thomas Magnum in "Magnum, P.I." The eight-season crime drama ran for nearly the entire decade, from 1980 to 1988, on CBS. It's old news at this point that the "Magnum" job cost Selleck the part of Indiana Jones in "Raiders of the Lost Ark," but the star never would have nabbed his iconic TV role had it not been for one of the best Western miniseries ever made , which he starred in opposite Sam Elliott: "The Sacketts."

When speaking with Ted Danson at a "Live Talks Los Angeles" event back in August, Selleck recalled the two-part Louis L'Amour adaptation. "I had also done by then a movie — a miniseries called 'The Sacketts,' which was a huge, huge break," the star explained. "So, they knew that I could handle a series." His work on the miniseries provided him with the chance to meet with several writers, including Donald P. Bellisario, ultimately leading to Selleck's vision for "Magnum, P.I."

"It's no exaggeration to say that 'The Sacketts' changed me," Selleck wrote previously in 2024's "You Never Know: A Memoir ― An Actor's Memoir of Hollywood and Television." He went on to add: "That job changed my professional opportunities and my whole outlook on what my appetites might be — and not only as an actor. In all of my life." In fact, the two-part Western led to an on-screen reunion only a few years later.

While the Sackett family was unavailable, L'Amour crafted a new family, the Travens, for his 1982 novel "The Shadow Riders" — and CBS jumped at the chance to get the posse back together. Unlike their previous Western, this horse opera was a made-for-TV feature, adapting only a single L'Amour novel — "The Sacketts" had tackled both "The Daybreakers" and "Sackett." For Selleck, that was more than enough.

"'The Shadow Riders' was not only a sacred trust but a dream come true," he noted. "Maybe that was better than a rest." Selleck shot "The Shadow Riders" between the second and third seasons of "Magnum, P.I.," marking the third and final Western he made with Elliott. The first? Well, Selleck got his first big break on the classic Western series "Lancer," ironically alongside his future co-star.

entertainment.title: Sweet Valley High's Twin Stars Made Their Acting Debut On A Beloved '60s Sitcom's Revival
entertainment.summary: The '90s show Sweet Valley High starred Cynthia and Brittany Daniel, but they made their TV debut as kids in the '80s on a revival of a classic show.
entertainment.body:
Gerardo Mora/Getty & undefined Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover The '90s introduced us to many great twin actors, but one duo fans may have forgotten is "Sweet Valley High" stars Cynthia and Brittany Daniel. "Sweet Valley High" — an adaptation of an immensely popular teen book series about blonde Californian identical twins Liz and Jessica Wakefield — was the Daniel sisters' breakout role, with roughly 2 million viewers tuning in to the 1st season. But fans may not know that the pair made their acting debut together on another show, "The New Leave It to Beaver."

"The New Leave It to Beaver," also known as "Still the Beaver," was the '80s revival of the beloved '60s sitcom "Leave It to Beaver." However, instead of following a young boy named Beaver as he grows up in a strange world, the sequel series follows Beaver as a divorced, single father of two trying to make ends meet under his new circumstances. "The New Leave It to Beaver" wasn't as successful as the original, which received two Emmy nominations.

At 13, Cynthia and Brittany Daniel appeared in the final season of "The New Leave It to Beaver," in an episode led by Beaver's son Ollie. In the episode, Ollie dreams of going on crazy adventures, including flying to another planet and meeting conjoined female aliens. The Daniel sisters played the alien girls, credited as Zorigna #1 and Zorigna #2, and wore a massive robe and green paint to make them look like conjoined aliens. In 2014, Brittany Daniel said of the role on Reddit , "It was hilarious! Serious blackmail footage!"

UPN/YouTube "Sweet Valley High" may have launched the Daniel sisters to fame, but they didn't become as iconic as Tia and Tamera Mowry , the Olsen twins, or the Sprouse twins. That's because they didn't build a career around their twin identity. "Sweet Valley High" turned the Daniel sisters into icons, with '90s kids envying their beach-filled lives.

But Cynthia Daniel mostly quit acting after "Sweet Valley High" was canceled after the 4th season, pivoting to a career in photography. Meanwhile, Brittany Daniel stuck with acting, leading to various roles in "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia," "That '80s Show," and "The Game." The pair went on to live two different lives.

Brittany said on Reddit that it was the right decision for them. "I would walk into an audition, and then she would walk in after me, and casting directors would say they could not make up their minds and were confused," she wrote. "... I think it helped us break into the business because we'd walk into the room, people would say, 'Oh wow, [there] are two of you, Doublemint Twins,' and then we got the role in 'Sweet Valley High,' but after a while we wanted to have our own identity." Cynthia has returned to acting twice since "Sweet Valley High," but both times were so she could play Brittany's twin again.

Speaking to Smashing Interviews Magazine , Melissa Rauch recalled her circumstances before auditioning for the role: "I was at the unemployment office the week before I got the job. I was thrilled to just get the audition for a one-time guest star role on 'Big Bang,' as I was a fan of the show. So, the fact that I am a regular part of the cast is something I am eternally grateful for."

Rauch blew everyone away at her audition. In Jessica Radloff's "The Big Bang Theory: The Definitive, Inside Story of the Epic Hit Series," showrunner and executive producer Steve Molaro recounts his impressions of Rauch : "Her reading was so different from everybody else's. She was funny and cute, and as she walked out, I remember we were all like, 'Whoa, she was great. Let's use her!'." Casting director Nikki Valko was even more enthusiastic about the future star, saying Rauch "knew where every beat was, every moment. It was a flawless audition, and that's the gold. And the role was only for one, maybe two episodes."

Rauch's Bernadette was introduced on October 19, 2009, in Season 3, Episode 5, "The Creepy Candy Coating Corollary," and became a series regular in Season 4. She remained on until the series finale, "The Stockholm Syndrome," and eventually had babies with Howard . She also recently appeared in "Stuart Fails to Save the Universe."

CBS According to Jessica Radloff's book, when Melissa Rauch saw how many people were auditioning for the role, she realized that she needed to stand out as much as possible. "There were so many girls auditioning, so I thought, I need to do something a little different. I had crappy $10 prop glasses in the glove compartment of my car for auditions," Rauch recalled, "so I decided to throw 'em in my bag just in case ..." The casting directors appreciated this subtle touch and recommended to Rauch's agent that she wear her glasses again at the table read. Rauch was eventually gifted the character's glasses as memorabilia after the show ended.

Bernadette's signature voice was also Rauch's idea. When asked by TV Insider how she came up with the voice, Rauch revealed that her mother was the blueprint: "My mother sounds very similar to Bernadette. She's got a very high-pitched voice except with a New Jersey accent, and I grew up imitating her." Rauch's little touches transformed Bernadette from a one-time guest into one of "The Big Bang Theory's" most iconic characters.

entertainment.title: Star Trek's Geordi La Forge Has A Heartbreaking Real-Life Story Behind His Name
entertainment.summary: Engineer Geordi La Forge of Star Trek: The Next Generation was named after a real-life Star Trek fan who passed away. His mother thanked Gene Roddenberry.
entertainment.body:
Paramount Television Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover There's more to LeVar Burton's Geordi La Forge than being an exceptionally dependable engineer, as the "Star Trek" character's name was inspired by a real person. Geordi worked aboard the USS Enterprise-D in all seven seasons of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" — which aired from 1987 to 1994 — and also appeared in later projects, like "Star Trek: Voyager" and "Star Trek: Picard."

When "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry and his team of writers came up with Geordi, they decided to honor the story of a passionate fan named Georgie LaForge, who tragically died in 1975 at age 19. Known for attending "Star Trek" fan conventions and loving the original "Star Trek" series , LaForge was quadriplegic and passed away from muscular dystrophy.

In a written correspondence in 1987 between Roddenberry and LaForge's mother, Sue LaForge, she thanked him on behalf of her family for paying tribute to her son. "It is an honor we would like to accept for him with the humility he so genuinely possessed," she wrote. "It was always a dream of his to be a part of the space program in some way. Never in his wildest dreams could he have hoped to be a part of the 'Star Trek' crew to represent the handicapped. How proud he would have been."

Paramount Television Gene Roddenberry and "Star Trek" didn't just honor Georgie LaForge through the name of Geordi La Forge. As fans know, the beloved "Star Trek" character is blind and initially wears a device called a VISOR over his eyes to help him see using electromagnetic signals. After "Star Trek: The Next Generation," Geordi trades his VISOR for similarly functioning eye implants that enabled actor LeVar Burton to play his role more comfortably.

The choice to make Geordi a character with a disability was intentional, considering that the "Star Trek" franchise lacked main characters with disabilities at the time and Roddenberry had wanted to include such a character to more accurately illustrate the vast diversity of humanity. "Diversity contains as many treasures as those waiting for us on other worlds," Roddenberry once said, according to StarTrek.com . "We will find it impossible to fear diversity and to enter the future at the same time."

Now, roughly four decades after Geordi La Forge emerged as both a groundbreaking character in "Star Trek" and a heartwarming tribute to a real-life individual, the franchise is commonly celebrated for its willingness to represent many walks of life in a futuristic sci-fi setting.

Visions of Sofia Wylie's Grace Franklin haunt the characters of Netflix's "The Body." Everything revolves around Grace in "The Body," as her falling into a coma following an ecstasy-laced initiation ritual for her Catholic high school's dance team triggers the group's psychological torment. Wylie has also had a couple of notable movie roles. In 2022, she starred as the young magic-wielder Agatha in Netflix's "The School for Good and Evil" film adaptation. Netflix/YouTube Audiences don't get to know Grace Franklin much in "The Body" before she enters a comatose state; however, her showstopping dance moves and somewhat nosy tendencies are apparent from the get-go. Wylie should have a lot more to do on-screen if Netflix renews "The Body" for Season 2, as Grace finally awakens from her coma in the Season 1 finale's closing moments. entertainment.title: 5 Beloved '60s Sitcoms That Deserve A Modern Remake
entertainment.summary: Some of the most beloved sitcoms ever made came out in the 1960s. Here are five that we would love to see get a modern-day remake.
entertainment.body:
ABC Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover While there are many examples of '60s television shows that couldn't be made today, there are several series from that era that are ripe for modern remakes, particularly when it comes to sitcoms. Many '60s sitcoms helped to shape pop culture, yet very few have been successfully revived as hits in the 21st century. That's a real shame, because there are a handful of '60s sitcoms that would actually work well in today's climate if they were remade the right way.

Of course, changing tastes need to be taken into consideration when choosing which '60s sitcoms to remake for modern audiences. For example, the war-themed sitcoms that were popular back then are unlikely to click with audiences today. But there were plenty of family-focused and fantasy sitcoms back then that could easily become big hits in the 2020s if they were only given the chance. Here are five '60s sitcoms that we would love to see brought back.

"The Addams Family," which for 64 episodes between 1964 and 1966 , parodies typical sitcoms by following a spooky family that has all the qualities of an All-American family in their own way. The humor comes from the culture clash between the Addams clan and regular people, who are often more normal but less family-focused than the Addams. The issue with the modern adaptations is that they've attempted to change the family's characteristics. The animated films reduce the Addams family's spooky factor to not alienate children, and the Netflix series is too obsessed with darkness and horror, forgetting there is a lot of mirth and hijinks to the characters.

We would love to see a remake of the '60s sitcom more in the vein of the '90s films starring Raul Julia and Anjelica Huston. We need a Gomez and Morticia with unmatched chemistry, a snarky Wednesday, and a violence-loving Pugsley thrust into the 21st century. Plus, a low-stakes sitcom about these well-known characters would allow creators to dive deeper into the family's strange customs while seeing them react to everyday things like social media. "Wednesday" shows that people still have a lot of love for "The Addams Family," so why shouldn't they get more?

Modern spy shows are generally very serious, so there's a big gap in the market for a small screen remake of "Get Smart." Perhaps interest in the franchise will spike after the upcoming movie reboot, which will star John Mulaney. Of course, the property has already been done on the big screen: Steve Carell played Maxwell Smart in 2008's "Get Smart," which pulled in over $230 million at the box office. Could a remake of the original sitcom also prove popular? We believe so. Older audiences would get the nostalgia of their beloved hit, while younger audiences would get something fresh.

entertainment.title: Tom Selleck Helped Launch This Short-Lived '80s Western Series With A TV Movie
entertainment.summary: Before he made his name as Magnum P.I., Tom Selleck landed a role as a wandering cowboy in a TV movie that would later spawn its own series.
entertainment.body:
Just before landing his breakout role in "Magnum, P.I.," Tom Selleck helped launch an ill-fated neo-Western series at CBS that you probably forgot all about. "Concrete Cowboys" hit the airwaves in October 1979, but it wouldn't morph into a series until two years later. The plot followed Selleck's former cowboy, Will Eubanks, and his partner J.D. Reed (Jerry Reed) as they travel from Montana to Nashville, only to find themselves in a heap of new trouble after being mistaken for detectives.

Although commonly thought of as an extended television pilot, Selleck himself dispelled that notion in his book, "You Never Know: A Memoir ― An Actor's Memoir of Hollywood and Television." According to the star, "Concrete Cowboys" wasn't initially meant to launch a series. "It wasn't a pilot, just a movie of the week," he explained. The 90-minute production offered Selleck the chance to work with Western legend Burt Kennedy, who directed the made-for-TV feature.

But Selleck maintained that the most memorable part of production had nothing to do with the film itself: "We were going to shoot the big bar fight, and it was going to take the entire day. On a TV budget, that's a big deal. It was the day John Wayne died." Like many, Selleck got his start in the Western genre , and Kennedy himself had been a frequent collaborator with the Duke. As he recalled, "Maybe John Wayne just might have been a little bit touched by what went on in that room on that day."

CBS That same year, Tom Selleck also starred in the Louis L'Amour adaptation "The Sacketts," one of the best Western miniseries ever made . His impressive body of work soon led to his role as Thomas Magnum, and "Concrete Cowboys" was left in the dust. So, when it was announced that the concept had been revived by CBS — with Jerry Reed returning — there were no hard feelings.

"The producers had no contract with me for a series, so they had recast my part," Selleck recalled. "And I wished them well." However, behind-the-scenes shake-ups between Universal and CBS threatened Selleck's vision for "Magnum, P.I.," sparking some doubt. "I only hoped I didn't find myself in the fall sitting home without a job, watching 'Concrete Cowboys,' knowing I could have been in it," he reflected in his memoir years later. Of course, it was the opposite that proved true.

"Concrete Cowboys" ran for only six episodes between February and March 1981 before the network pulled the plug. Geoffrey Scott took over Selleck's role as Will Eubanks, but Reed — playing a revamped J.D. Reed — was more the focus this time around. The result was essentially a "Route 66" rip-off, as the two former cowboys traveled the country finding themselves in more trouble than ever. As for Selleck, "Magnum, P.I." ran for eight seasons on CBS.

entertainment.title: 15 Most Underrated Family Guy Episodes, Ranked
entertainment.summary: Family Guy has hundreds of episodes for viewers to sort through, meaning there are plenty of diamonds in the rough for you to discover.
entertainment.body:
Fox Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover After decades on the air, it's no surprise that "Family Guy" has some truly legendary episodes to its name. However, any list of the best "Family Guy" episodes is going to feel a little incomplete, as some episodes simply make a bigger splash than others. It's high time some adventures finally get their due, so let's honor the most underrated "Family Guy" episodes that deserve your attention just as much as "PTV."

When you think of a classic "Family Guy" episode, you probably imagine rapid-fire cutaway gags, non-stop jokes, and an irreverent sense of humor. Some episodes abide by these qualities well; they just fail to make as much of an impression in viewers' minds as others. Other installments try to break away from the typical formula. This doesn't always land, but you have to admire when a show is willing to swing for the fences.

When ranking the most underrated episodes of "Family Guy," we tried to find the best of the best that don't normally crop up on "Best Of" lists. These are the diamonds in the rough that have gone ignored for far too long.

Fox Over the years, "Family Guy" has referenced and parodied a lot of films and TV shows from the 1980s. As such, it only makes sense for the sitcom to go all in on the decade with Season 20's "80's Guy."

Peter (Seth MacFarlane) becomes obsessed with the '80s, landing himself and Chris (Seth Green) in a lot of trouble. Lois (Alex Borstein) eventually chews him out, which offers some excellent meta commentary on the show as a whole. It's almost as though Lois is being used as a mouthpiece by the writers to say how tired they are of referencing the decade and want to move onto other things.

Meanwhile, there's another plot where Stewie (MacFarlane) and Doug (Chris Parnell) bond over a mutually beneficial expedition to rescue their frisbee from a jungle gym. The two stories work perfectly together: one stuffed to the brim with pop culture references, and the other a more grounded, emotionally driven adventure. They work in tandem to ensure the episode never goes off the rails, and it's a great late-stage outing from "Family Guy."

Fox When you think of "Family Guy" humor, you probably think of cutaway gags right away. "Family Guy" popularized the format by cramming early episodes with a ton of non-sequitur jokes. A character, usually Peter, would compare a situation to something ridiculous, and then we'd jump scenes to see the scenario play out. Some think it's hilarious while others may find it to be a crutch, but no matter what side you land on, you'll probably laugh at "Cutawayland."

entertainment.title: William Shatner Believes CBS Made A Big Mistake Canceling His Short-Lived Sitcom
entertainment.summary: William Shatner has always been passionate about his roles, so when CBS canceled his 2010 sitcom, he made it very clear that he thought it was the wrong move.
entertainment.body:
During an interview with Vulture , the actor opened up about the show's demise and minced no words about the network's logic. "They shouldn't have canceled '$#*!My Dad Says;' it was too popular. And we were getting it right. I don't know what happened in CBS's mind," Shatner told the outlet. "I'm told that it's in the top 10 in Canada, and here it was in the top 20 most of the time; it was in the top 25 all the time. So, I don't understand that."

Adapted from Justin Halpern's viral, profanity-laced Twitter feed, "$#*! My Dad Says" followed a broke, struggling young writer who is forced to move back in with his outspoken, cranky father. Produced by David Kohan and Max Mutchnick, the duo behind "Will and Grace," the series starred Jonathan Sadowski as Henry Goodson alongside Shatner as the opinionated patriarch Ed Goodson. The cast also featured Will Sasso, Nicole Sullivan, and Stephanie Lemelin. Despite getting off to a strong start, ratings eventually dwindled, with CBS pulling the plug right as they were just getting started. Shatner, however, was baffled by the decision.

According to TV Series Finale , while the show drew over 12 million viewers for its premiere and earned a solid 4.0 rating, there was a noticeable drop with following episodes, with it ultimately averaging a respectable 3.0 rating in the key 18–49 demographic.

CBS/YouTube Despite those decent numbers, CBS reportedly chose to prioritize co-owned properties like "Rules of Engagement" for syndication potential, with "$#*! My Dad Says" getting put on the chopping block after a single 18-episode season.

While the fact that the show had solid ratings and even snagged a People's Choice Award for Favorite New TV Comedy in 2011 may have given William Shatner the impression that all was well with "$#*! My Dad Says," it appears no one filled him in on the "$#*!" critics were saying. The show — which also made our list of shows we can't believe existed — holds a dreaded 0% score on Rotten Tomatoes, with the audience score coming in at a not-so-impressive 55%.

Among the bloodbath of negative reviews, the San Francisco Chronicle panned the premise from inception to pilot, declaring that turning 140-character rants from a cranky old man into a fully formed sitcom was nearly impossible, no matter how much the laugh track tried to make you think otherwise. Meanwhile, Variety dismissed the show as a formulaic comedy dragged down by limp one-liners. However, they did at least credit Shatner as the one providing some spark. The outlet highlighted that the TV veteran made the pilot barely watchable by bringing a dose of poignant warmth to his bombastic role, even if the surrounding material wasn't up to par.

entertainment.title: Why Don Knotts Left The Andy Griffith Show
entertainment.summary: Don Knotts played Barney Fife on The Andy Griffith Show, but left the show as a series regular after Season 5. Here's why the star left the show.
entertainment.body:
For those who have somehow never come across an episode on MeTV or TV Land, "The Andy Griffith Show" was a beloved CBS TV series that followed the easygoing Sheriff Andy Taylor (played by the late Andy Griffith ) as he kept the peace in the sleepy, tight-knit fictional town of Mayberry. His trusty sidekick, and arguably one of the funniest TV characters of all time , was Barney Fife, the quirky deputy sheriff best known for his frantic energy, trembly voice, and his inflated sense of self-importance. The role earned Don five Emmy Awards, which leads fans to question: Why would he leave a role that earned him such accolades?

As revealed by Don Knotts' daughter, Karen Knotts, her father's exit after the show's fifth season stemmed from a combination of exhaustion and a massive career opportunity. "Put yourself in his place. That show was hard, hard work," Karen told Woman's World during an exclusive interview. "Then think of the character, and also the energy that it took to play him. Imagine the intensity, plus the level of perfection that was being strived for."

According to Woman's World, both Don and Griffith were always on the same page about wrapping up "The Andy Griffith Show" after five seasons — which ended up not being the case — so when Universal swooped in with a lucrative five-picture film deal, Knotts took the leap, though leaving the series behind brought him a severe case of anxiety.

If his resume is any indication, venturing to the big screen proved fruitful for Knotts, who went on to star in films like "The Reluctant Astronaut." As Karen recalled of her father's forward-moving philosophy, "He never was one to go back and look at stuff from the past. He loved the show, but he would just look at each new project for what it was and take it for what it was." Following Don's exit from "The Andy Griffith Show," producers brought in comedian Jack Burns for Season 6 to play deputy Warren Ferguson, though the character failed to connect with audiences and was quietly written out. But for Don, the door to Mayberry never fully closed. He eventually returned as Barney Fife for five special guest appearances during the show's subsequent seasons.

entertainment.title: 15 Best Cartoon Villains In TV History, Ranked
entertainment.summary: Throughout the history of animated shows, there have been some memorable villains, and these are the best cartoon antagonists we've come across.
entertainment.body:
Disney XD Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Whether an animated series is made for kids or adults, there has to be a great antagonist at the center of all the action. These are the best TV villains in cartoon history who continue to inspire fear and, oftentimes, a lot of laughs.

It's not just action-oriented shows that benefit from having bad guys. Even comedies need some kind of foil for the main character to bounce off of. They can be a boss, business rival, or even an all-powerful cosmic being who has a penchant for rearranging all of the holes on a person's face.

The best villains can prepare children for the evil that inevitably exists in the real world. And they can show adults that the bad guy ruining their day isn't really all that bad in the grand scheme of things. Most TV bad guys are just normal humans, but with animation, a truly great villain can be anything. So, let's rank the best cartoon villains of all time.

Nickelodeon Every so often, Plankton (Mr. Lawrence) from "SpongeBob SquarePants" will set his sights on world domination (or at least conquering Bikini Bottom). But for the most part, he's just a little guy trying to get his hands on the Krabby Patty secret formula. As the seasons have gone on, his plans have become way more convoluted, so you never know what kind of Rube Goldberg contraption he'll come up with next.

And even though "SpongeBob SquarePants" has been on the air for decades now, Plankton has remained reliably consistent all that time. While other characters have become flanderized, like Patrick becoming extremely stupid, Plankton is still just an evil microscopic organism who thinks he's smarter than everyone else.

We even get some backstory on Plankton and how he used to be friends with Mr. Krabs (Clancy Brown), but the two had a falling out. This adds an extra layer of depth amid all of the jokes. Plankton adding some much-needed chaos to "SpongeBob SquarePants" undoubtedly helps make the show one of the best Nickelodeon cartoons ever .

ABC Cartoon villains tend to have a lot less nuance than live-action ones. They typically fall into the mustache-twirling bad guy trope, but that's where David Xanatos (Jonathan Frakes) from "Gargoyles" changes everything.

He's a billionaire who's actually modeled off of Bruce Wayne. The idea was what if you took this guy who has near-limitless resources and no desire to take over the world. He just wants to achieve his own personal goals, which often run counter to what the gargoyles want to achieve.

entertainment.body:
DFree/Shutterstock Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Everyone knows Indiana Jones is one of Harrison Ford's most iconic roles. It's easy to picture the adventurous character wearing his leather jacket and holding his signature bullwhip. But instead of Ford, imagine Tom Selleck under Jones' trademark fedora. Believe it or not, that image was almost what film audiences got. But thanks to "Magnum, P.I.," it never came to be, and Ford owes his famous character to Selleck and his series.

With his signature moustache and Hawaiian shirt, Tom Selleck's role as Thomas Magnum is instantly recognizable. Years before dining with his uniformed family on "Blue Bloods," his investigative side was privatized, and he carried a much lighter sense of humor.

After filming the pilot for "Magnum, P.I.," Selleck got a call from his agent to read for the role of Indiana Jones in "Raiders of the Lost Ark." After a subsequent callback, Steven Spielberg and George Lucas offered him the part. But, as the movies show, he would not go on to portray the famous archaeologist. After Selleck backed down from the part, Spielberg suggested Ford for the role. The rest is history.

Kathy Hutchins/Shutterstock When Tom Selleck was offered the role for "Raiders of the Lost Ark," he had already filmed the "Magnum P.I." pilot "Don't Eat the Snow in Hawaii." He was vocal about this with George Lucas and Steven Spielberg, who were apparently surprised at his honesty. Six weeks later, while the offer was still standing, CBS had purchased "Magnum, P.I." While Selleck wanted to play both roles, CBS refused, believing he would end up quitting the series.

Selleck, despite his thoughts towards the show's title and the changes he suggested that made it what it was , does not regret playing the private eye. He still advocates that he wouldn't have quit playing Magnum if allowed to do both roles, but understood CBS' hesitance. "That was a big disappointment," Selleck told Esquire when discussing the missed role. "But it wasn't like "Magnum" was a consolation prize. The fact that Steven Spielberg and George Lucas wanted me, and that I could do this kind of stuff — big-time iconic leads — was a great sense of security and confidence."

sports.title: Knee surgery complicates Puka Nacua's future
sports.summary: Timeline for recovery make mean he won't be 100 percent before free agency.
sports.body:
Via ESPN, the recovery time following surgery to repair the MCL tear is four to five months . If accurate, that ends Nacua’s 2026 season.

The problem becomes 2027. Nacua is in the last year of his rookie contract. He hasn’t gotten a second deal, due in large part to the off-field issues that recently resulted in a three-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy and that culminated in an offseason stay at an in-patient holistic rehab facility after he was “ drowning myself ” in alcohol.

Based on the ESPN report, Nacua won’t be back to 100 percent before free agency starts. The Rams will have to decide whether to sign him to a new deal, to apply the franchise tag (or the transition tag), or to let him become a free agent.

The injury makes it very difficult for Nacua to land in the Jaxon Smith-Njigba ballpark ($42.15 million per year), even though Nacua’s skills and abilities justify that type of deal.

The situation becomes a prime example of the extent to which off-field issues can complicate a player’s financial interests. Without the New Year’s Eve incident that resulted in a lawsuit and, eventually, a diversion program and, inevitably, a suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy, Nacua would have had his second contract by now. Or, at a minimum, he would have had greater standing to hold out (or hold in) until he got paid what he deserves.

Instead, Nacua continued to carry the injury risk into the final year of his rookie contract. And the injury risk became reality 13 days ago, when McVay dialed up a running play to Nacua on third and 11 while trying to run out the clock in a 20-13 game against the Commanders.

It’s a win for the Rams, who may be able to keep Nacua for a lot less than it would cost to give him a market-level contract. However the Rams play the situation, Nacua’s knee injury will make it easier, and cheaper, to re-sign him.

Ultimately, Nacua may have to prove in 2027 that he is back to full strength. And he may have to get through a full season unscathed to unlock the long-term deal his performances earned — but his off-field complications squandered.

The combined record of 27-10 equates to a success rate of 73 percent — the highest by any division through Week 10 in NFL history.

Outside the division, the teams of the NFC North are 21-4. The 84-percent success rate is the most for any division through Week 10 since the AFL-NFL merger.

This weekend, the Lions host the Bucs, the Bears host the Saints, and the Vikings face the 49ers in Mexico City.

In theory, all four teams could make the playoffs. That would require the fourth-place team landing higher in the standings than the second-place team in each of the other three divisions.

And that makes Wednesday night’s game between the 6-4 Packers and 6-4 Rams critical to the outcome of the chase for the wild-card berths in the NFC.

sports.title: Aidan Hutchinson wasn't fined for sack that injured Drake Maye
sports.summary: As expected, Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson wasn't fined for the tackle that may have ended Patriots quarterback Drake Maye's season.
sports.body:
The weekly announcement from the league includes no fines against Hutchinson.

A question emerged as to whether Hutchinson’s sack of Maye amounted to a hip-drop tackle. During the broadcast, Fox rules analyst (and former NFL senior V.P. of officiating) Mike Pereira said it wasn’t a hip-drop tackle. On Monday, NFL in-house rules analyst Walt Anderson confirmed that it wasn’t a hip-drop tackle .

But it’s not Anderson who makes the decisions on fines. Jon Runyan makes those decisions. Not surprisingly, Runyan decided that the tackle was not a violation of the rules.

Under the rules, a hip-drop tackle happens when a player “grabs the runner with one or both hands or wraps the runner with both arms; and . . . unweights himself by swiveling and dropping his hips and/or lower body, landing on and/or trapping the runner’s leg(s) at or below the knee.” Anderson said Hutchinson did not “unweight” himself or “swivel.”

Hutchinson suffered a torn ACL in his knee while celebrating the sack. Although it’s not clear whether Maye will play again in 2026, Hutchinson is done for the year.

sports.summary: Lamb was praised for the block by the league's website and by Tom Brady, but the disciplinary process said he used his helmet.
sports.body:
“Can’t-Miss Play: CeeDee Lamb’s HUGE block springs Pickens free for 39-yard TD,” the caption on the highlight video says.

Calling the play on Fox, Tom Brady praised Lamb, immediately recognizing it as a great downfield block.

But the league’s disciplinary process didn’t think it was so great. Lamb has been fined $23,882 for what the NFL deemed “Unnecessary Roughness: Use of the helmet.”

Lamb confirmed to reporters on Thursday that he had been informed he was getting fined, but he insisted he didn’t make contact with his helmet and found it frustrating that receivers take hits routinely but get fined when they make one.

“I can block, and I’m real good at doing things like that, but I get fined,” Lamb said. “I never touched him with my helmet. . . . I guess as a receiver, we can get hit, but can’t deliver the punishment.”

Lamb will surely appeal the fine for what looked, both to the league’s website and the league’s all-time greatest player, like a good block.

sports.body: Grappling with injuries on defense, the Buffalo Bills have elevated linebacker Shaq Thompson and cornerback Tre’Davious White from their practice squad ahead of Sunday’s matchup with the Miami Dolphins. [Media: https://twitter.com/SalSports/status/2124255025832562722?a=XSKVjMjfw1qXVM1Adj0&s=20] Thompson, 32, played in 12 regular-season games for Buffalo last season, starting 6. He totaled 56 tackles, 1 sack, 6 tackles for loss, 2 pass breakups, and 1 fumble recovery. In Buffalo’s two playoff games, Thompson was excellent, notching 13 total tackles, a team-high 10 solo tackles, 2 tackles for loss, and an interception. The veteran is a former first-round pick of the Carolina Panthers, having been the No. 25 overall selection in the 2015 NFL Draft. Thompson will have a role this week in place of Dorian Williams, who is out with a calf injury that he suffered late in last week’s win over the New York Jets. Whether Thompson plays a significant role on defense or not is yet to be determined, but at worst, he provides strong depth for the Bills. Rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr is the other likely option to start next to Terrel Bernard. White, 31, also spent last season with the Bills. He played a significant part in the team’s defense, starting 16 games in the regular season across from Christian Benford. It’s thanks to Benford’s injured groin that White finds himself elevated this week, as he’ll either start across from rookie Davison Igbinosun or serve as depth behind the second-year man that he started over last season, Maxwell Hairston. During the 2025 season, White totaled 40 tackles, 10 pass breakups, and an interception. In the postseason, White started both games, totaling six tackles and three pass breakups. White originally entered the NFL in 2017 as Buffalo’s first-round draft choice that year, and after spending the 2024 season with the Baltimore Ravens and Los Angeles Rams, he returned home and played well last season. White allowed just 51% of the pass thrown when he was the closest man in coverage to be completed, holding opposing quarterbacks to a 71.1 quarterback rating when targeting him. The Bills and Dolphins are a 1 p.m. EDT start on Sunday. Each team’s official inactive lists will be released 90 minutes prior to kickoff.

sports.title: Will Shane Steichen be back in 2027?
sports.summary: After the 2025 season ended, Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon put both G.M.
sports.body:
Then, one day after the Colts lost to the Titans in Week 6, she fired Ballard and kept Steichen.

Nearly five weeks later, Steichen remains. After next Sunday’s game against the Giants, the Colts will enter their bye. That’s typically the best time for an in-season coaching change, since it gives the interim coach maximum time to get up to speed before the next game.

Creating a vacancy with six weeks left in the regular season carries a separate benefit. The team can get a head start on searching for the replacement. And if ownership already knows the coach will be fired after the season ends, it makes no sense to delay that part of the process.

So here’s the question. Will Irsay-Gordon bring Steichen back in 2027?

It makes no sense to keep a new G.M. from hiring a new coach. Every G.M. arrives with a wish list of coaches who would be pursued, if/when the position is vacant. It makes plenty of sense to give a new G.M. an immediate vacancy to fill.

But what about the Colts this year has made sense? The firing of the G.M. left the team without a seasoned, experienced executive to navigate the strategy of making, or not making, trades. They quickly moved guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. They rejected offers for running back Jonathan Taylor and quarterback Daniel Jones. They moved two starting receivers — Keenan Allen and Josh Downs — on the day of the trade deadline.

Steichen has been operating for much of the season with one hand tied behind his back. Now, he’ll have both wrists secured. Whatever the decision will be as to Steichen, it’s unfair to base it on the team’s overall performance since the Nelson and Buckner trades.

Before that point, they took the Chiefs to overtime in Kansas City. They beat the Texans. They manhandled the Commanders in London. They took the Vikings to the limit in Minnesota.

sports.body: The injuries continue piling up for the Buffalo Bills ahead of their Week 11 home game against the Miami Dolphins. A surprise report originating from the team on Saturday afternoon revealed that Bills starting defensive tackle Ed Oliver is dealing with an oblique injury. Oliver is now listed as questionable for Sunday’s home game, though the news is not all doom and gloom. Matt Parrino provided some context to Oliver’s injury, tweeting that “(p)er a league source, Ed Oliver notified Bills training staff this morning that he felt pain in his oblique. The staff checked it out and there’s optimism that he’ll play against the Dolphins.” Per NFL rules, Oliver’s ailment must be accounted for on the injury report even at this late stage, which is why he’s being listed as questionable. In the past, Oliver’s situation would have likely had him tabbed as “probable” for game day. The NFL has since done away with that injury designation, which has seen the questionable term pick up the slack in filing injuries throughout the league. Should Oliver be unable to go (or limited in some fashion) it would be a huge blow to Buffalo’s defense, which already has to account for injuries to starters in cornerback Christian Benford and inside linebacker Dorian Williams. Both Bills defenders have been ruled out ahead of Week 11.

A rare Sunday where I get to wait until 4pm to be utterly disappointed instead of the classic 1:00 devastation. I figured the Jets hadn’t been to SoFi too often, but I was shocked to learn that they haven’t been there since two trips in 2020. The first trip should sound fairly familiar: a Week 11 contest between two terrible teams that had only two combined wins. The Jets employed an old journeyman QB with no tangible long-term future with the team, and the Chargers had Justin Herbert. Had the Chargers not won this past Monday, this would’ve been the exact description of both Jets vs. Chargers games at SoFi Stadium. The second trip was much more memorable: the 0-13 Jets faced a talented 9-4 Rams team and shocked the world by finally winning their first game of the season. We all remember this as the game that shifted the Jets’ odds of having the first overall pick when every poor fanbase was looking to ‘Tank For Trevor’. The Jets won the following week and finished 2-14, securing the second overall pick and failing to properly tank. For those of you who value tanking so much, the Jets have an opportunity to repeat history by winning a game in SoFi Stadium and dropping further down the draft board. sports.body: The Buffalo Bills host the Miami Dolphins on Sunday in a game of two franchises headed in completely opposite directions. The 8-1 Bills sit atop the AFC, leading the conference by one game over the Jacksonville Jaguars and Kansas City Chiefs (the Denver Broncos are also 7-2, but they are currently the No. 5 seed in the playoff picture). Miami, on the other hand, is 1-8 and tied for the AFC’s worst record with the Los Angeles Chargers and Tennessee Titans. On paper, this a game that Buffalo should win running away. However, games are played on the field, not on paper, and Miami has kept plenty of games close this season. Half of Miami’s losses have come in one-possession games, and they’ve held great offenses like the Chiefs and the Detroit Lions under their season scoring average. Shutting Gordon down and keeping Miami in continuous second-and-long or third-and-long scenarios will go a long way towards driving the Bills to victory this week. In 17 matchups with No. 17 at the helm against Miami, the Bills are 14-3. They know about it now, and they have the resources to fully investigate.

sports.title: Daiyan Henley being out with a knee injury changes nothing about the failed trade to Broncos
sports.summary: The failed trade of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley returned to the front burner on Friday, with the news that Henley will miss Sunday's game against the Jets due to a knee injury.
sports.body:
It was a knee condition that prompted the Broncos to pull the plug on the deal — after trying to renegotiate the terms after the trade deadline.

From Mike Klis of 9News, who covers the Broncos: “Chargers ILB Daiyan Henley missed entire week of practices with knee injury and has been ruled out for game vs Jets. This validates concerns raised by Broncos medical team and GM George Paton. And proves Chargers were not on the up and up .”

Does it really prove that the Chargers weren’t “on the up and up”? The issue is that the Denver physical flagged a knee problem. In lieu of finding that the physical had been failed and that the trade won’t happen, the Broncos were willing to give Henley a passing grade, if the compensation was changed.

Henley has played every game this season. He played on Monday night against the Ravens. As far as anyone knows, he injured the knee during that game.

As far as anyone knows, the currently injured knee isn’t the same knee that created the concern during the Denver physical.

It’s all just noise at this point. The core problem is the ability of a team — after the trade deadline has passed — to renegotiate the terms of a trade. And the related issue is the ability of a team to give a conditional grade on the pass-fail question of a physical that is tied to the specific compensation.

A player either passes the physical, or he fails it. The process shouldn’t include an epilogue premised on the outcome of the physical being “maybe.” Especially after the time for negotiating trades has ended.

sports.title: Raiders owner Mark Davis hated the Madden movie
sports.summary: Did anyone read the script before allowing the Raiders' name and logo to be used?
sports.body:
The Raiders owner teed off on the Madden movie , in an interview with John Katsolimetes of the Las Vegas Review-Journal .

“My comment is, it’s full of turducken,” Davis said initially.

“It depends on whether you like turducken or not, and obviously, I don’t like turducken,” Davis said.

“I think it’s really it’s unfair to take people that have passed away and make caricatures out of them, and try to sell it as truth,” Davis said. “They start the movie with a statement saying that all of it’s not true, but some of it is, so it’s confusing what to believe.”

That’s not an uncommon device. “Based on a true story” means that plenty of liberties will be taken in an effort to make the story more compelling.

Mark Davis had one specific concern regarding the shading of the truth. He objected to his father’s reaction to the serious neck injury suffered by Patriots receiver Darryl Stingley, during a preseason game in 1978.

“So John goes over to the hospital afterwards, you know, and really looks after him,” Mark Davis said, “and there’s a scene where my dad is telling John, ‘You don’t need to go over there. You don’t need to take care of other teams’ players. You take care of our players.’

“That’s just so far from the truth. Anybody who has ever known him knows my dad always took care of people behind the scenes. If it was a player from another team had an issue that wasn’t being taken care of, my dad would quietly take care of that even if it was players on other teams. I’m serious. . . . It just it felt cheap to me to build up John’s image at the expense of my father’s.”

sports.title: NFL didn't know Puka Nacua had surgery when agreeing to suspension
sports.summary: The sudden decision of the NFL to suspend receiver Puka Nacua three games raises plenty of relevant questions.
sports.body:
After Rams coach Sean McVay disclosed to reporters that Nacua had surgery to repair a torn MCL suffered during a Week 9 win over the Commanders, Judy Battista of NFL Network reported this: “The NFL did not know Puka Nacua had had knee surgery on Tuesday when it suspended him yesterday.”

Surely, that’s accurate; Judy is a solid reporter. But that extra fact doesn’t matter to the NFL’s ultimate handling of Nacua.

The report creates the impression that, during the negotiations that resulted in the three-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy, Nacua and/or his representatives withheld material information. That, at some level, the league had been duped by the lack of knowledge that Nacua had undergone surgery that will sideline him for “a couple months.”

First, the suspension (as the league affirmatively explained on Thursday) is separate from the injury. The NFL listed multiple examples of players who served suspensions while injured.

Second, whether Nacua (who had already missed one of the four minimum games he’s required to miss while on IR), was already going to serve the entirety of the suspension while on injured reserve with or without surgery.

Third, the surgery and the extended absence actually avoids the possibility that Nacua would have returned to action exactly one game after finishing his suspension, resulting in no net games missed due to the suspension.

The mere existence of the report represents an implicit acknowledgement by the league that the negotiated suspension, aimed at allowing Nacua to double-dip when it comes to his stint on injured reserve and his suspension, underscores the broader question of whether players should be allowed to serve a suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy when otherwise unable to play. That’s a separate issue for the NFL to revisit, if it chooses, through a potential revision to the terms of the policy.

As explained on Friday, the league could have refused the deal. It could have insisted on pushing the issue through the full process, with Judge Sue L. Robinson conducting a hearing and the outcome potentially being appealed (by Nacua and/or the league) to the Commissioner. But that would have entailed a non-zero-percent chance that Nacua wouldn’t have been suspended at all.

sports.title: Jaguars saw something in Liam Coen that other teams didn't
sports.summary: The Jaguars identified Coen as their No. 1 candidate and re-shaped their front office to get him, at a time when other teams weren't even interviewing him.
sports.body:
Coen’s great success should have other teams that hired new head coaches in 2025 asking themselves: What did we miss? Because the Jaguars were so high on Coen that he was their No. 1 target and they were willing to do whatever it took to get him, while no other team even bothered to give Coen an interview.

During the 2025 NFL coaching search , we tracked dozens of reports of head coaching interviews and requests among the seven teams that had vacancies. The Jaguars were the only team that so much as asked Coen to interview.

This week there’s been some media scrutiny on the Jets, who hired Aaron Glenn without considering Coen as a candidate. Glenn is 5-22; Coen is 20-6. But it’s unfair to single out the Jets for failing to interview Coen, because no team other than the Jaguars did, either.

The 41-year-old Coen had a résumé that should have made him a good candidate. NFL teams are always on the lookout for coaches who can nurture a franchise quarterback and run an innovative offense. Coen played quarterback at UMass and coached quarterbacks in college before getting hired by Sean McVay to work on the Rams’ staff, eventually became the Rams’ offensive coordinator under McVay, and had been a successful playcaller as offensive coordinator for the Buccaneers, as well as at Kentucky. With that background, it’s surprising that only the Jaguars wanted him.

And the Jaguars really wanted him, to the point that they were willing to do whatever it took to hire him. Coen initially turned the Jaguars down and agreed to a contract extension to stay with the Buccaneers, but Jaguars owner Shad Khan wouldn’t take no for an answer. When Coen said he was concerned about the direction of the Jaguars’ front office, Khan fired General Manager Trent Baalke and agreed to reshape the front office in a way that Coen would approve of if Coen would take the job. Coen was persuaded to take the Jaguars job, and the Jaguars later hired James Gladstone, who had worked with Coen on the Rams, as GM.

The result has been the Jaguars going from one of the worst teams in the NFL to one of the best. Coen’s success in Jacksonville has justified the faith Khan had in him. And raises questions about the total lack of interest from the rest of the league.

sports.body: The Buffalo Bills and Miami Dolphins have been seeing each other twice a year since 1966, and over those 60 years, both teams have had their turn making life miserable for the other. In the early years, Miami dominated the rivalry, winning championships and making trips to the Super Bowl. Then came the Jim Kelly-Dan Marino era, when two future Hall of Fame quarterbacks battled for AFC supremacy. Kelly and the Bills made four consecutive Super Bowl appearances while Marino never returned after his lone trip following the 1984 season. These days, the rivalry belongs mostly to Buffalo. Since Josh Allen arrived in Western New York in 2018, he’s gone 14–3 against Miami, including a playoff victory. The Dolphins have managed to sneak in three wins — just enough to make Allen and the rest of Bills Mafia angry before the next meeting. But the Dolphins coming to Buffalo this week look very different from the team that challenged the Bills’ hold on the AFC East just a couple of seasons ago. Tua Tagovailoa, Tyreek Hill, and Jaylen Waddle are gone. So are Minkah Fitzpatrick and Bradley Chubb, who now wears a Bills uniform. De’Von Achane is still in Miami but sidelined with an injury. And with starting quarterback Malik Willis also on injured reserve, Kyle McCord is preparing for just his second NFL start. Miami may have a new look, but that doesn’t mean everyone on its sideline is unfamiliar with Buffalo. Several members of Jeff Hafley’s coaching staff have faced the Bills in previous stops around the league, while others have crossed paths with the coaches now leading Buffalo. sports.body: The Indianapolis Colts were blown out on Thursday Night Football by the Houston Texans. The defeat dropped Indianapolis to 3-8 on the season. As we move into the weekend, the Colts’ first round pick is currently sixth overall. Of course that is relevant as the Jets own that pick from last year’s Sauce Gardner trade. There is currently a big logjam of teams with three to four wins. An Indianapolis victory would have dropped their pick outside the top ten even if only temporarily. In the first round, the Jets have their own selection, Indianapolis’, and whichever pick is higher between Dallas’ and Green Bay’s selections. According to Tankathon, the Jets currently own three of the top twelve picks in the 2027 NFL Draft. Here is the current order. - Titans 1-8 - Chargers 1-8 - Dolphins 1-8 - Jets 2-8 - Eagles 2-7 - Jets (from Colts 3-8) - Cardinals 3-7 - Falcons 3-7 - Buccaneers 3-6 - Saints 3-6 - Commanders 3-5-1 - Jets (from Cowboys 4-6) - Texans 4-6 - Ravens 4-6 - Raiders 4-6 - Patriots 5-5 - Seahawks 6-4 - Browns (from Rams 6-4) Picks 19 through 32 are determined by the results of NFL Playoff games.

sports.body: The New York Jets versus Los Angeles Chargers matchup is a huge contest in the Week 11 slate. How do I know? They’re the only game scheduled for 4:05 pm ET on Sunday, November 22. Is that because the NFL wanted to put them in a temporary standalone window? No, it’s probably only because this game is being played on the West Coast — but it’s still important! That is because of the implications for the 2027 NFL Draft. The Jets are 2-8 and the Chargers are 1-8. The Athletic’s Austin Mock explained how a win or loss would impact both teams’ odds of landing the No. 1 overall pick: ”A Jets loss would bump their odds of getting the No. 1 pick to 10 percent, while a win would almost certainly knock them out of that race. Meanwhile, a Chargers loss would put them firmly back in contention for the top pick, at 23 percent, whereas a win would leave them at just 7 percent. That’s the biggest result this week for draft purposes.” So this is a must-lose game for the Jets? Are we even allowed to call it that? --- J-E-T-S! Take the game-day conversation with you!
